deep.reconstruction:
This is a two-page spread. The left page (p. 274) is the end of the preceding paper in the volume. It holds a table of decimal values of q^n/n! for n = 15,…,31. Checking n = 15 against the printed 6.68803×10^-10 gives q = π/2 (since (π/2)^15/15! ≈ 874.6/1.3077×10^12 ≈ 6.688×10^-10). The closing remark says these powers are divided by the same factorials with which powers of π occur in the earlier formulas, so the decimal evaluation is easier. This is a series-evaluation aid, presumably for sine/cosine-type series in π.

The right page (p. 275) opens E598 with §1, which is introductory only. Euler praises Lagrange's memoir in the Berlin Academy's volume for 1773 (the 'Recherches d'arithmétique') on the divisors of the general binary quadratic form Btt+Ctu+Duu. He says that because Lagrange's treatment is so general, less practised readers find it hard. He therefore proposes two things:
(i) to lay out every step of the proofs and specialize them to simpler forms, which the next page does for pp+nqq, showing that divisors are represented by forms frr+grs+hss with 4fh−gg=4n;
(ii) to assess how far this supports the many theorems he had found only by induction, and so what is still missing for complete proofs.
There is no mathematics proper on this page beyond the table.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an introductory paragraph plus the tail of a numerical table from another paper. Euler's reception of Lagrange's 1773 work in E598 is well documented in histories of the theory of quadratic forms (Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History).
transcription_corrections: Left-page table entries read as q^n/(1·2·…·n), with q = π/2 judging from the values (e.g. q^15/15! = 6.68803…×10^-10).
Right page: 'vnde multo clarius parebit' – the '[?]' is unnecessary; the text reads 'multo clarius'.
